{{Short description|Subset of irreversible thermodynamics}}
{{Thermodynamics|cTopic=systems}}

'''Endoreversible thermodynamics''' is a subset of irreversible [[thermodynamics]] aimed at making more realistic assumptions about [[heat transfer]] than are typically made in [[reversible process (thermodynamics)|reversible]] thermodynamics. It gives an upper bound on the power that can be derived from a real process that is ''lower'' than that predicted by Carnot for a [[Carnot cycle]], and accommodates the [[exergy]] destruction occurring as heat is transferred irreversibly. 

It is also called '''finite-time thermodynamics''', '''entropy generation minimization''', or '''thermodynamic optimization'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bejan |first=Adrian |date=1996-02-01 |title=Entropy generation minimization: The new thermodynamics of finite-size devices and finite-time processes |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |language=en |volume=79 |issue=3 |pages=1191–1218 |doi=10.1063/1.362674 |issn=0021-8979|doi-access=free |bibcode=1996JAP....79.1191B }}</ref>

== History ==
Endoreversible thermodynamics was discovered multiple times, with Reitlinger (1929),<ref>H.B. Reitlinger, ''Sur l'Utilisation de la Chaleur dans les Machines à Feu'' (Vaillant-Carmane, Liège, 1929), p. 25</ref> Novikov (1957)<ref>Novikov, I. I. "Efficiency of atomic energy installation." ''Atomnaya Energiya'' 3.11 (1957): 409-412.</ref><ref name="Novikov1958">{{cite journal | last1 = Novikov | first1 = I.I. |  year = 1958 | title =  The efficiency of atomic power stations (a review) | journal = Journal of Nuclear Energy | volume = 7 | issue =1–2 | pages = 125–128 | doi=10.1016/0891-3919(58)90244-4}}</ref> and Chambadal (1957),<ref name="Chambadal1957">Chambadal P (1957) ''Les centrales nucléaires''. Armand Colin, Paris, France, 4 1-58</ref> although it is most often attributed to Curzon & Ahlborn (1975).<ref name="Curzon1975">{{cite journal | last1 = Curzon | first1 = F.L. | last2 = Ahlborn | first2 = B. | year = 1975 | title =  Efficiency of a Carnot engine at maximum power output| journal = American Journal of Physics | volume = 43 | issue = 1 | pages = 22–24 | doi=10.1119/1.10023| bibcode = 1975AmJPh..43...22C}}</ref> 

Reitlinger derived it by considering a heat exchanger receiving heat from a finite hot stream fed by a combustion process.

A brief review of the history of rediscoveries is in.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vaudrey |first1=Alexandre |last2=Lanzetta |first2=François |last3=Feidt |first3=Michel |date=2014-12-01 |title=H. B. Reitlinger and the origins of the efficiency at maximum power formula for heat engines |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/jnet-2014-0018/html |journal=Journal of Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics |language=en |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=199–203 |doi=10.1515/jnet-2014-0018 |issn=1437-4358|arxiv=1406.5853 |bibcode=2014JNET...39..199V }}</ref>

== Efficiency at maximal power ==

[[File:NovikovEngine.png|500px|thumb|right|Novikov engine showing irreversible heat transfer between <math>T_H</math> and <math>T_{iH}</math>, coupled to a [[Carnot cycle]] operating between <math>T_{iH}</math> and <math>T_C</math>.<ref name="Wagner2008"/>]]
Consider a semi-ideal [[heat engine]], in which heat transfer takes time, according to [[Thermal conduction|Fourier's law of heat conduction]]: <math>\dot Q \propto \Delta T</math>, but other operations happen instantly.

Its maximal efficiency is the standard Carnot result, but it requires heat transfer to be reversible ([[Quasistatic process|quasistatic]]), thus taking infinite time. At maximum power output, its efficiency is the '''Chambadal–Novikov efficiency''':

::<math>\eta = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{T_L}{T_H}} = 
1-\sqrt{1-\eta_{Carnot} }  </math>

Due to occasional confusion about the origins of the above equation, it is sometimes named the '''Chambadal–Novikov–Curzon–Ahlborn efficiency'''.
[[File:Chambadal–Novikov efficiency.svg|thumb|306x306px|The plot of Chambadal–Novikov efficiency as a function of Carnot efficiency. We see that it is always less than Carnot efficiency, but approaches it at the two ends.]]

=== Derivation ===
This derivation is a slight simplification of Curzon & Ahlborn.<ref name="Curzon1975" />

Consider a heat engine, with a single [[working fluid]] cycling around the engine. On one side, the working fluid has temperature <math>T_H'</math>, and is in direct contact with the hot heat bath. On the other side, it has temperature <math>T_L'</math>, and is in direct contact with the cold heat bath.

The heat flow into the engine is <math>\dot Q_H = k_H(T_H - T_H')</math>, where <math>k_H</math> is the [[Thermal conduction|heat conduction coefficient]]. The heat flow out of the engine is <math>\dot Q_L = k_L(T_L' - T_L) </math>. The power output of the engine is <math>\dot W = \dot Q_H - \dot Q_L</math>.

Side note: if one cycle of the engine takes time <math>t</math>, and during this time, it is in contact with the hot side only for a time <math>t_H</math>, then we can reduce to this case by replacing <math>k_H</math> with <math>k_H \frac{t_H}t</math>. Similar comments apply to the cold side.

By Carnot theorem, we have <math>\eta = \frac{\dot W}{\dot Q_H} \leq 1 - \frac{T_L'}{T_H'}</math>. This then gives us a problem of constraint optimization:<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\max_{T_H', T_L'} \dot W \\
\frac{\dot W}{\dot Q_H} \leq 1 - \frac{T_L'}{T_H'}
\end{cases} </math>This can be solved by typical methods, such as [[Lagrange multiplier|Lagrange multipliers]], giving us<math display="block">T_H' = x\sqrt{T_H}; \quad T_L' = x\sqrt{T_L}; \quad x = \frac{k_H\sqrt{T_H} + k_L\sqrt{T_L}}{k_H + k_L}</math>at which point the engine is operating at efficiency <math>\eta = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{T_L}{T_H}}</math>.

In particular, if <math>k_L \gg k_H </math>, then we have <math display="block">T_H' = \sqrt{T_HT_L}; \quad T_L' = T_L </math>This is often the case with practical heat engines in power generation plants, where the work fluid can only spend a small amount of time with the hot bath (nuclear reactor core, coal furnance, etc), but a much larger amount of time with the cold bath (open atmosphere, a large body of water, etc).

=== Experimental data ===
For some typical cycles, the above equation (note that [[absolute temperature]]s must be used) gives the following results:<ref name="Curzon1975" /><ref name="Callan1985">Callen, Herbert B. (1985). Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics (2nd ed. ed.). John Wiley & Sons, Inc.. {{ISBN|0-471-86256-8}}.</ref>

<!-- copied from [[Heat engine]]: -->
{| class="wikitable"
! ''Power Plant'' !! <math>T_L</math> (°C) !! <math>T_H</math> (°C) !! <math>\eta</math> (Carnot) !! <math>\eta</math> (Endoreversible) !! <math>\eta</math> (Observed)
|-
! [[West Thurrock]] ([[United Kingdom|UK]]) [[Fossil fuel power plant|coal-fired power plant]]
| 25 || 565 || 0.64 || 0.40 || 0.36
|-
! [[CANDU reactor|CANDU]] ([[Canada]]) [[nuclear power plant]]
| 25 || 300 || 0.48 || 0.28 || 0.30
|-
! [[Larderello]] ([[Italy]]) [[Geothermal power|geothermal power plant]]
| 80 || 250 || 0.33 || 0.178 || 0.16
|}

As shown, the endoreversible efficiency much more closely models the observed data. 

However, such an engine violates Carnot's principle which states that work can be done any time there is a difference in temperature. The fact that the hot and cold reservoirs are not at the same temperature as the working fluid they are in contact with means that work can and is done at the hot and cold reservoirs. The result is tantamount to coupling the high and low temperature parts of the cycle, so that the cycle collapses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lavenda |first=B. H. |date=2007-02-01 |title=The thermodynamics of endoreversible engines |url=https://pubs.aip.org/ajp/article/75/2/169/1056299/The-thermodynamics-of-endoreversible-engines |journal=American Journal of Physics |language=en |volume=75 |issue=2 |pages=169–175 |doi=10.1119/1.2397094 |issn=0002-9505|arxiv=cond-mat/0604094 |bibcode=2007AmJPh..75..169L }}</ref>  

In the Carnot cycle, the working fluid must always remain constant temperatures, as the heat reservoirs they are in contact with and that they are separated by adiabatic transformations which prevent thermal contact. The efficiency was first derived by William Thomson<ref name="Thomson1853">W. Thomson, Phil. Mag. (Feb. 1853)</ref> in his study of an unevenly heated body in which the adiabatic partitions between bodies at different temperatures are removed and maximum work is performed. It is well known that the final temperature is the geometric mean temperature <math>\sqrt{T_HT_L}</math> so that the efficiency is the Carnot efficiency for an engine working between <math>T_H</math> and <math>\sqrt{T_HT_L}</math>.

An introduction to endoreversible thermodynamics is given in the thesis by Katharina Wagner.<ref name="Wagner2008">M.Sc. Katharina Wagner (2008), ''A graphic based interface to Endoreversible Thermodynamics'', TU Chemnitz, Fakultät für Naturwissenschaften, Masterarbeit (in English). http://archiv.tu-chemnitz.de/pub/2008/0123/index.html</ref> It is also introduced by Hoffman et al.<ref>K. H. Hoffmann. An introduction to endoreversible thermodynamics. Atti dell Accademia Peloritana dei Pericolanti - Classe di Scienze Fisiche, Matematiche e Naturali, pages 1–19, 2007.</ref><ref name="Hoffman1997">{{cite journal | last1 = Hoffmann | first1 = K. H. | last2 = Burzler | first2 = J. M. | last3 = Schubert | first3 = S. | year = 1997 | title = Endoreversible Thermodynamics | journal = J. Non-Equilib. Thermodyn. | volume = 22 | issue = 4| pages = 311–355 }}</ref> 

A thorough discussion of the concept, together with many applications in engineering, is given in the book by Hans Ulrich Fuchs.<ref name="Fuchs2011">H. U. Fuchs, ''The Dynamics of Heat'' (2nd ed.), chapter 9. Graduate Texts in Physics, Springer 2011, {{ISBN|978-1-4419-7603-1}}</ref>
